title: Landlord Insurance: Buy-to-Let, Rent & Liability Cover
description: Landlord insurance explained: buildings and landlord contents, liability, loss of rent, US DP-3 policies and what to tell your insurer about tenants.
intro: A standard home insurance policy usually stops covering a property once you let it out. Landlord insurance is built for rented homes: the building, your furnishings, liability to tenants and visitors, and optional loss of rent.

blocks.title: Landlord cover at a glance
covered: Buildings: fire, storm, flood, escape of water, subsidence
Landlord’s contents in furnished lets (carpets, white goods, furniture)
Property owner’s liability if a tenant or visitor is injured
Loss of rent or alternative accommodation for tenants after an insured event
excluded: Rent arrears from a tenant who simply stops paying (needs rent guarantee)
Damage during long empty periods beyond the policy limit

sections.html: Standard home insurance assumes the policyholder lives in the property. Letting it out changes the risk: different people, longer empty periods, and legal duties as a landlord. If you let a property on a home policy without telling the insurer, claims can be refused. That includes “accidental landlords” renting out a home they couldn’t sell, and people letting a room to a lodger (tell your home insurer; some will adapt your policy).

sections.h2: Loss of rent vs rent guarantee
sections.html: Loss of rent pays rent you lose when the property can’t be lived in after an insured event such as a fire or flood. Rent guarantee insurance is different: it covers rent arrears when a tenant doesn’t pay, usually only if the tenant passed referencing before the tenancy started. Read the conditions carefully, including how quickly you must report arrears.

US landlords usually insure single-family rentals on a dwelling fire policy such as the DP-3 (open-perils cover for the dwelling) or a landlord package. These typically include fair rental value (loss of rent) and can add premises liability. Tenants are encouraged to buy their own renters insurance for their belongings.

• Portfolio landlords can often insure several properties on one policy with a single renewal date.
  • HMOs (houses in multiple occupation) need insurers who accept them; licensing conditions may also apply.
  • Short-term and holiday lets need specialist cover; standard landlord policies usually assume longer tenancies.
  • Commercial property lets (shops, offices) need commercial property insurance.

faqs.q: Is landlord insurance a legal requirement?
faqs.a: No, but buy-to-let lenders require buildings cover, and landlords have legal duties to tenants that make liability cover sensible.

faqs.q: Does landlord insurance cover tenants’ belongings?
faqs.a: No. Tenants need their own contents or renters insurance.

faqs.q: What if my property is empty between tenants?
faqs.a: Most policies restrict cover after a set number of consecutive days unoccupied. Tell your insurer; see our guide to unoccupied property insurance.
